design_detail: Four fatal cases identified by the authors in Finland during 2000 and 2001, described from the history that could be obtained, a post-mortem examination and toxicology of blood and urine (with hair and tablet analysis in case 2). Each death was certified by a forensic pathologist as a combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide. The journal labels the paper a case report. How the four were found, and whether other deaths with MDMA or with other drug combinations in the same period were reviewed, is not stated.
can_establish: That MDMA and moclobemide were found together in the blood of four young people who died suddenly in one Finnish region in 2000 and 2001, none of whom had been prescribed moclobemide, with the course that bystanders and hospital staff could describe (confusion, convulsions, collapse, in one a body temperature of 43.2 °C) and with the forensic pathologists’ judgment that the combination caused each death.
cannot_establish: How often the combination causes death or serotonin toxicity (no denominator: the people who took both and lived, or all deaths involving MDMA, are not counted); whether serotonin toxicity rather than the other substances found in all four people (and, in case 2, dextromethorphan at roughly 28 to 110 times the paper’s quoted reference range) caused the deaths; what amounts were taken or why the drugs were combined; or anything about the clinical signs that define serotonin toxicity, which were not recorded.

sample.recruitment: Other: deaths identified by the authors (forensic medicine departments in Helsinki and Turku, an accident and emergency department in London and a provincial state office) as appearing to be a fatal interaction between MDMA and moclobemide; how they were found is not stated (Method, p. 365). All four were from one region (Province of Western Finland) and cases 1 and 2 occurred within a short time of each other (Discussion, p. 367).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Deaths in which MDMA and moclobemide were both found and judged by the authors to be a fatal interaction; no other criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: Case 1, woman aged 18; case 2, man aged 23, who appears to have taken several drugs and had old needle marks, whose hair held MDMA and amphetamine from the previous 1.5 to 2.5 months; case 3, man aged 18 who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years; case 4, man aged 19. For case 1 there was no evidence of mental illness or prescription medicines (p. 366). Moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the four (p. 367).
sample.selection_effects: Selected by outcome and by the presence of both drugs: only deaths are described, so the series shows what was found in people who died and says nothing about the many who may have taken both and did not die. The cases come from the authors’ own forensic departments in one region over two years. Almost all the information comes from post-mortem toxicology and a pathologist’s judgment, with only sparse accounts from bystanders and hospital staff.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem blood and urine toxicology (headspace gas chromatography for alcohol; thin-layer chromatographic screening of urine; quantitation of 150 drugs in blood by gas chromatography with nitrogen detection or by mass spectrometry; confirmation by mass spectrometry), hair analysis in case 2 and analysis of the recovered tablets in case 2 (both types held MDMA and no other active substance). Tablets in the other cases were not analysed in the paper: in case 3 they were named ecstasy by a friend at the scene (Method, pp. 365–366; Cases, p. 366).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known for any case; recorded only as case conditions. Case 1: an unknown quantity of street ecstasy; case 2: two kinds of white tablets found (marked 666 or with a star), amounts not stated; case 3: tablets named ecstasy and a pack of moclobemide 300 mg tablets prescribed to a friend, amounts taken not stated; case 4: the paper states ten ecstasy tablets were taken, without giving the source of this history, and the moclobemide amount is not given. Post-mortem blood concentrations in mg/L, MDMA then moclobemide: case 1, 1.6 and 2.3; case 2, 2.0 and 2.1; case 3, 1.7 and 7.9; case 4, 2.1 and 6.5. The paper quotes a reference range of 0.1 to 0.35 mg/L for MDMA and 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L for moclobemide and calls moclobemide a maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and a moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4. Editors’ calculation: the four MDMA concentrations are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the quoted MDMA range.
exposure.polysubstance: Present in all four. Case 1: alcohol (printed as 0.65 g/dL in blood and 0.69 g/dL in urine) and amphetamines in urine. Case 2: dextromethorphan 1.1 mg/L (quoted reference range 0.01 to 0.04), morphine 0.08, amphetamine 0.1, cyclizine 0.3, oxazepam 1, diazepam 1, desmethyldiazepam 0.1 and temazepam 0.2 mg/L, traces of alprazolam; the pathologist considered dextromethorphan a contributor to the death. Case 3: amphetamine 0.15 mg/L, MDA 0.05 mg/L, THC 1.8 µg/L, urine alcohol 0.28 g/dL with none in blood, amphetamines and cannabinoids in urine. Case 4: MDA 0.05 mg/L, THC 3.1 µg/L, lidocaine 1.6 mg/L, no alcohol (Cases, p. 366 and p. 367). The paper does not weigh the other substances in cases 1, 3 and 4.

comparison.controls: None. The paper makes no comparison with deaths from MDMA alone, moclobemide alone or other combinations.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history (stated only for case 1), time between taking the drugs and the collapse (stated only loosely, case 1 the next morning), the setting and activity, fluid intake, and, for cases 1, 2 and 4, body temperature.

outcomes.instruments: Autopsy with histology, toxicology (above) and the history from bystanders and hospital staff; the cause of death was certified by a forensic pathologist in each case (M.J. for cases 1 and 3, T.S. for case 2, P.W. for case 4), and all three are among the authors.
outcomes.validity_norms: No clinical criteria for serotonin toxicity (Sternbach’s or the Hunter rules) are applied. The authors say that the mode of death was consistent with serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it, although the history and clinical observations were limited in most cases (Discussion, p. 367). No post-mortem finding specific to serotonin toxicity is reported: autopsy found no evident cause of death in cases 1 to 3 and, in case 4, oedematous lungs with general visceral congestion.
outcomes.operationalization: Death attributed to a combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide; the authors then describe the mode of death as consistent with serotonin syndrome. The clinical features given: case 1, sudden confusion, convulsions, loss of consciousness and cessation of breathing, no temperature taken; case 2, a confused state before being found dead; case 3, sudden confusion, rolling about on the floor, then collapse, with a body temperature of 43.2 °C (when it was taken is not stated); case 4, found unconscious with breathing difficulties, no temperature available.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The pathologists who certified the deaths are among the authors, and the cases were identified because both drugs were present.

analysis.effect_sizes: None calculated and none possible: four selected deaths and no denominator. Ages 18 to 23 (one woman, three men). Blood concentrations (mg/L), MDMA then moclobemide: 1.6 and 2.3; 2.0 and 2.1; 1.7 and 7.9; 2.1 and 6.5. Editors’ calculation: MDMA 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end (0.35 mg/L) of the reference range the paper quotes; moclobemide 0.9 and 0.8 times the upper end of its quoted range (2.5 mg/L) in cases 1 and 2 and 3.2 and 2.6 times in cases 3 and 4. The paper states that the risk of death is high when another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAOI, is taken with MDMA (Discussion, last paragraph, p. 367), without a rate or a comparison.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A case report; no protocol or registration applies.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cases were identified because both drugs were present; deaths in the same period with MDMA alone or with other drugs are not described, so the series cannot show how the combination compares. For cases 2 and 4 no body temperature was available and for no case are clonus, reflexes, tone or tremor recorded.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four young people who died suddenly in Western Finland in 2000 and 2001, blood contained MDMA (1.6 to 2.1 mg/L, several times the paper’s quoted reference range) and moclobemide (2.1 to 7.9 mg/L); all had other substances too, moclobemide had been prescribed to none of them, forensic pathologists called each death a combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the sparse histories (confusion, convulsions, collapse; one body temperature of 43.2 °C) are described by the authors as consistent with serotonin syndrome.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the probable cause of death in each case was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs, that each person seems to have taken moclobemide to enhance the effects of MDMA, and that warnings are needed against misinformed attempts to potentiate illicit drugs (p. 365); the Discussion states that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAOI, is taken with MDMA (p. 367). Gaps: (1) the pathologists’ stated cause was combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs; serotonin syndrome is the authors’ reading of limited clinical information, and no examination finding that defines it was recorded; (2) the abstract’s seems to have taken the drug to enhance the effects sits against the Discussion’s statement that it is not known why the victims combined the substances (p. 367); (3) other substances were present in all four and are not excluded as contributors, in case 2 including dextromethorphan; (4) a high risk of death rests on four selected deaths with no denominator; (5) all four MDMA concentrations were well above the paper’s quoted reference range, and the paper does not say whether MDMA alone at those concentrations could have caused the deaths.

timeline.event: This paper: four fatal cases described; by the authors’ knowledge no fatal case of MDMA with moclobemide had been reported before (Discussion, p. 367).
Gillman restates the four deaths in a review and says that he knows of several unpublished cases of MDMA with an MAOI (as read for this library; the unpublished cases are not described).

Silins and colleagues cite these cases among a handful of case reports of deaths with MAOIs and MDMA, and rank MAOIs with MDMA at the highest level of risk in a review that did not appraise study quality (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: The two later reviews read for this library restate this series and add no counted cases (Gillman 2005 mentions unpublished ones without detail); no series with a denominator, and no clinical series with examination findings, was found among the sources read. The literature outside them was not searched, so this card does not say that none exists.

funding.declared_conflicts: None declared; the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are from the forensic medicine departments of the Universities of Helsinki and Turku, an academic accident and emergency department in London and the Provincial State Office of Western Finland (p. 365); the pathologists who certified the deaths are among them. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study with a denominator: poison-centre, emergency-department and forensic records from several countries that count every presentation or death involving MDMA, with and without a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (moclobemide and others), noting whether the inhibitor was a prescribed medicine, recording the examination findings that allow the Hunter criteria to be applied, blood concentrations and other substances, and comparing the combination with MDMA alone and with MDMA plus other serotonergic medicines.

domains.note: No comparison group, and every person had other substances in the blood (alcohol, amphetamines, THC; in case 2 dextromethorphan and several sedatives); MDMA alone at 4.6 to 6.0 times the quoted reference range cannot be excluded as the cause.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Post-mortem concentrations, not amounts taken or timing; tablets analysed in one case only; the source of moclobemide is known in one case (a friend’s prescription); concentrations after death may not match concentrations during the illness.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Selected by death and by the presence of both drugs, found by the authors’ departments in one region over two years, with no statement of how.
Resuscitation was attempted in cases 1 to 3 and hospital care is not described for case 4; whether treatment altered the findings is not stated.
The history is limited in every case; no body temperature in cases 1, 2 and 4; no examination finding (clonus, reflexes, tone, tremor) in any; no urine screen in case 4.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Cause of death is a pathologist’s judgment, made by authors who selected the cases for the combination; autopsy found no evident cause in cases 1 to 3; serotonin syndrome is not diagnosed against any criteria.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: A case report with no protocol; all four cases are described in detail, but deaths with other drug combinations in the same period are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: METHODS 5.3 lists no instrument for case series, and the card schema asks for one; ROBINS-E, the tool for non-randomized studies of exposures, was used as the closest fit, with the lack of any comparison group counted under confounding. Two domains are very high and three high: the series has no comparison, no denominator, other substances in every person and a cause of death that is a judgment by authors who picked the cases. The source may be cited as a record that four deaths with MDMA and moclobemide in the blood were reported from Finland, with the pathologists’ conclusion and the sparse clinical details. It may not be cited for how often the combination kills, for serotonin toxicity as the proven mechanism of these deaths, or for the combination being worse than MDMA alone.

key_findings.finding: Four deaths in Finland in 2000 and 2001 that appeared to the authors to be due to an interaction between MDMA and moclobemide. As detailed a history as possible was obtained and a post-mortem examination was carried out in each, with toxicology samples.

Laboratory methods: alcohol by headspace gas chromatography in blood and urine; urine screened for several hundred substances by thin-layer chromatography; blood monitored for 150 drugs by gas chromatography with nitrogen detection; confirmation and quantitation by mass spectrometry. The quoted reference range is 0.1 to 0.35 mg/L for MDMA in blood and 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L for moclobemide; the limit of quantitation for MDMA in blood was 0.04 mg/L.
key_findings.locator: Method (the same paragraph, continued from p. 365)

key_findings.finding: Case 1: woman aged 18 who took an unknown quantity of street ecstasy one night; the next morning she became suddenly confused, convulsed, lost consciousness and stopped breathing; resuscitation failed; no temperature was taken. Autopsy found no evident cause of death. Blood MDMA 1.6 mg/L and moclobemide 2.3 mg/L; blood alcohol printed as 0.65 g/dL and urine alcohol 0.69 g/dL; amphetamines in urine. The pathologist gave the cause of death as combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide.

Case 2: man aged 23 found dead after a confused state, with two kinds of white tablets (both contained MDMA and nothing else active) and old needle marks; no cause of death at autopsy. Blood MDMA 2.0, moclobemide 2.1, dextromethorphan 1.1 (quoted reference range 0.01 to 0.04), morphine 0.08, amphetamine 0.1, cyclizine 0.3, oxazepam 1, diazepam 1, desmethyldiazepam 0.1 and temazepam 0.2 mg/L; hair held MDMA and amphetamine from the previous 1.5 to 2.5 months. The pathologist gave combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide as the cause and considered dextromethorphan a contributor.

Case 3: man aged 18, who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years, who became suddenly confused at a friend’s apartment, rolled about on the floor and collapsed; resuscitation failed; tablets named ecstasy by a friend were found with a pack of moclobemide 300 mg tablets prescribed to the friend; body temperature of the deceased 43.2 °C. Blood MDMA 1.7, amphetamine 0.15, MDA 0.05 and moclobemide 7.9 mg/L, THC 1.8 µg/L; urine alcohol 0.28 g/dL with none in blood. The pathologist gave combined accidental poisoning with moclobemide and MDMA as the cause.

Case 4: man aged 19 who, the paper states, had taken ten ecstasy tablets; he was unconscious with breathing difficulties at a health centre and died in hospital; no further history or temperature. Autopsy: oedematous lungs and general visceral congestion. Blood MDMA 2.1, MDA 0.05, moclobemide 6.5 and lidocaine 1.6 mg/L, THC 3.1 µg/L; no alcohol; no urine drug screen because of small sample volume. The pathologist gave combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide as the cause.
key_findings.locator: Case 4 (begins at the foot of p. 366)

key_findings.finding: Moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the four people; it was at maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and in moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Moclobemide had not been prescribed

key_findings.finding: Editors’ calculation: the four blood MDMA concentrations (1.6, 2.0, 1.7, 2.1 mg/L) are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the reference range the paper quotes (0.35 mg/L); the dextromethorphan concentration in case 2 (1.1 mg/L) is roughly 28 to 110 times its quoted range (0.01 to 0.04 mg/L).
key_findings.locator: Method (reference ranges) and Cases 1 to 4 (calculated by the editors)
key_findings.note: Editors’ calculation. What population the quoted reference ranges describe is not stated.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that, to their knowledge, no fatal cases of MDMA with an MAO-A inhibitor such as moclobemide had been reported, and that, although history and clinical observations were limited in most cases, the mode of death in each was consistent with serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it.

The authors state that it is not known why the victims combined the substances; that the only known connection between the cases is the region, with cases 1 and 2 close in time; that case 2 appears to have taken several drugs; and that moclobemide could in case 2 also have slowed the breakdown of dextromethorphan and so added to the serotonergic effect.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning It is not known why the victims combined these substances

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAO inhibitor, is taken together with MDMA, and that many public sources minimize the risk of death from interactions.
key_findings.note: A statement without a denominator or comparison; the series itself shows four deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the probable cause of death in each case was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs. The pathologists’ stated cause in all four is combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide, and the Discussion says only that the mode of death was consistent with serotonin syndrome, with limited history and clinical observations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Serotonin syndrome is the authors’ interpretation of sparse bystander accounts, not a finding recorded by an examiner; no feature that defines it (clonus, reflexes, tone, tremor) is reported for any person.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that it seems each person took moclobemide to enhance the effects of MDMA; the Discussion says it is not known why the victims combined the substances.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intent is not known in any case; the one case with a known source (a friend’s prescription, case 3) does not show why it was taken.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 1’s alcohol is printed as 0.65 g/dL in blood and 0.69 g/dL in urine, a blood level that would be many times the legal driving limit and potentially fatal on its own; in case 3 blood held no alcohol while urine held 0.28 g/dL. The paper does not comment on either, or on alcohol as a contributor.
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit in case 1 is probably a misprint (for example g/L), which is the editors’ inference and not stated in the paper; as printed, alcohol would be a competing cause of death in case 1, and either way its role is not weighed.

reporting_issues.issue: All four MDMA concentrations (1.6 to 2.1 mg/L) are 4.6 to 6.0 times the upper end of the reference range quoted in the Method (0.1 to 0.35 mg/L); the paper does not discuss whether MDMA at these concentrations could have caused the deaths without moclobemide. Case 2 also had dextromethorphan at roughly 28 to 110 times its quoted range, which the pathologist considered a contributor.
reporting_issues.consequence: Attributing the deaths to the interaction rests on judgment; the paper gives no comparison with MDMA deaths at similar concentrations without moclobemide.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract describe four deaths after MDMA and moclobemide, but the toxicology shows other drugs in every case (case 2 had at least eight other substances and old needle marks), and lidocaine in case 4 (1.6 mg/L) is unexplained; the explanation given for lidocaine in case 1 is resuscitation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The series is of deaths with MDMA and moclobemide present among other substances, not of deaths from the pair alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the risk of death is high with an MAO inhibitor and MDMA; the paper counts four deaths and gives no number of people who took the combination or of other MDMA deaths in the region and period.
reporting_issues.consequence: No rate or relative risk can be derived; the statement is an opinion supported by four selected cases.

reporting_issues.issue: The clinical information needed to apply the Sternbach or Hunter criteria is missing: body temperature was recorded only for case 3 (43.2 °C, with no statement of when it was taken relative to death), and no case records clonus, reflexes, tone, tremor or sweating.
reporting_issues.consequence: The deaths cannot be classified against either set of criteria; the temperature in case 3 is the only sign that points toward heat-related illness, and it is not tied to a time.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 365–368 (full text: abstract, introduction, Method, the four cases, Discussion, reference list); units of the concentrations (including the THC values in micrograms per litre) were checked against a page render. The earlier case reports and the website pages the paper cites were not read.
